I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

issues.item: Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future
issues.explanation: 'Talking about the future' is a weak and atypical trigger for a life-threatening accident in this profile, and it lacks a clear clinical link to the rest of the selected memory, threat, and appraisal items. The other triggers are interpersonal/victim-related, but this item suggests a different theme that is not supported elsewhere.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: 'Checking if someone is following me' implies pursuit/interpersonal threat. In a life-threatening accident profile, this is hard to reconcile with the rest of the report, which otherwise reflects generalized danger, hypervigilance, and trauma-memory disturbance rather than a specific persecutory/following threat.

issues.item: Triggers: Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
issues.explanation: For a 58-year-old fisherman with a life-threatening accident, 'Reminders of victims' implies exposure to multiple casualties or dead/injured others. That is not impossible, but it is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise reads like a personal survival-focused accident trauma rather than a mass-casualty/witnessing-victims presentation.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: The memory profile is dominated by disorganized, present-tense reliving ('Cannot Find Words', 'Feels Present Not Past'), which fits severe PTSD, but 'intense rage' on recall points to a qualitatively different emotional tone that is not supported elsewhere by the triggers, threat, or appraisals. With no corroborating anger/blame themes, this item stands out as internally and cross-node incongruent.

vignette:
Harjit Sandhu is a 58-year-old widowed South Asian fisherman who presented for his first psychological assessment following a referral from his primary care physician, who had grown concerned about the marked deterioration in Harjit's functioning over the preceding fourteen months. He lives alone on the Gulf Coast, where he has worked the water since his mid-twenties, and he came to the intake appointment quietly, choosing a seat near the door and spending much of the first session looking past the clinician's shoulder toward the window.

Fourteen months ago, Harjit was driving home along a two-lane coastal highway after selling his catch at the docks. It was early evening, the light already thinning, and the road was nearly empty. A pickup truck crossed the center line without warning and struck his vehicle head-on. The impact was catastrophic. Harjit's door was crushed inward, trapping his left leg; the cab filled with the smell of fuel and the hiss of something under the hood. He remained conscious throughout, pinned in silence - an eerie, total silence that settled after the initial crash before any sirens came - certain he was going to die there alone in the dark. Rescuers worked for nearly forty minutes to free him. He sustained multiple fractures and internal injuries requiring surgery and a prolonged hospital stay. The driver of the other vehicle, a young man, did not survive.

In the weeks that followed, Harjit noticed that the memory of those forty minutes did not behave the way he expected a memory to behave. When it returned - and it returned often - it did not feel like something he was recalling. It felt like something that was still happening. The crush of metal, the smell of fuel, the silence pressing in around him: they arrived with the same terror he had felt on the highway, not softened by distance or time. He found, when he tried to describe any of this to his physician or to his adult daughter, that the words simply were not there. He knew exactly what had happened, but when he opened his mouth, the experience seemed to exist in a register that language could not reach, and he would fall quiet and change the subject.

Harjit had always been a man who moved through the world with a certain quiet confidence, someone his crewmates described as steady. That person had become unrecognizable to him. He was certain, in a way he could not fully articulate, that his body had become unreliable - that it might fail him without warning, as it nearly had on the highway - and this conviction had quietly reshaped how he moved through each day. He no longer trusted himself to read his own physical signals. He had also come to feel that people were not what they seemed, that the ordinary social world concealed something he had been naive to miss before. Talking to strangers, which his work had always required - buyers at the dock, harbor officials, the rotating crew members who came and went - now produced a tightening in his chest and a vigilance he could not suppress. He found himself watching faces too carefully, listening for something he could not name.

On the water, which had once been the one place he felt most himself, he found that unusual stillness - a flat calm, the engine cut, the kind of silence that fishermen generally welcome - produced the same dread he had felt pinned in that car. He began avoiding solo runs and then began calling in sick on days when he could not find a reason to go out at all. Over twelve months he lost two contracted buyers who needed reliable supply, and his income dropped significantly. At home, even in his own kitchen, he remained on guard, scanning the room when he entered, listening at the walls. When his daughter visited and the conversation turned, as it sometimes did, to the young man who had died in the crash, or to any talk of people losing someone they loved, Harjit would excuse himself and not return to the room.

What finally brought him to seek help was a conversation with his daughter in which she told him, gently and with evident grief, that she felt she had lost him too. He had sat with that for several weeks before making the appointment. What he feared most, he said near the end of the intake, was that the man he used to be was simply gone. What he hoped, though he offered it tentatively, was that someone might help him find out whether that was actually true.
